description: We are ALTARIS, a team of six passionate innovators with backgrounds in artificial intelligence, software development, data analysis, and engineering. Driven by curiosity and a shared passion for technology, we aim to transform complex data into meaningful insights. Through NASA Space Apps, we seek to explore Earth's changing systems, uncover hidden patterns, and develop creative, impactful solutions to real-world challenges.
summary:
A few wet or dry years are not a rainfall trend. ALTARIS is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web tool that helps students, farmers and local planners in Central America ask the detective’s question: how much confidence does this trend deserve?

Built on 24 years (2001–2024) of NASA GPM IMERG satellite rainfall, it covers 4,332 map cells of about 11 km across seven countries. Each cell gets an evidence verdict (consistent, limited or none) from Mann–Kendall and Theil–Sen tests, adjusted for testing thousands of places at once. Every verdict is stress-tested across different year windows, El Niño/La Niña years and the 2014 satellite change, and compared with NASA POWER at the case sites. We also calibrated the method on pure random noise to check that it does not invent trends, so the tool is open about what the data cannot show.

Users choose a season and a place, step through the years, read plain-language reasons, and open the statistical detail and a downloadable evidence passport. Three guided examples show that even a result that passes every test can remain an open question. In a region where rainfall variability shapes farming decisions, ALTARIS helps separate signal from noise before anyone acts on it. It describes the past; it makes no forecasts.
details:
What it does

ALTARIS answers one question: how much confidence does a rainfall trend deserve? Rainfall naturally rises and falls from year to year, so a line that slopes down for a few years is not always a trend. Users pick a season (May–October, July–August or the whole year) and tap any of 4,332 map cells of about 11 km, covering Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador, Belize, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. They see the year-by-year rainfall, the estimated trend with its margin of error, and an evidence verdict: consistent, limited or no evidence, with the reasons written in plain language. They can choose the start and end years and watch the story change, then open the statistical detail (Theil–Sen slope, Mann–Kendall p-value, FDR-adjusted p, confidence interval) and export an evidence passport with the data, method and limits.

Who it helps

The challenge points to students and the public. ALTARIS is a free bilingual (English/Spanish) tool for students, farmers, communities and local planners. A first-visit guide, a guided tour of the whole page, a “?” help marker on every zone and short definitions make it usable without statistics training, while the technical detail stays one click away for people who want to audit it.

Intended impact

To make "how sure are we?" the first question people ask before acting on a rainfall trend, so students, farmers and local planners do not over- or under-react to a few wet or dry years, and so the evidence behind any claim can be checked and shared.

Why it is different (and creative)

Most tools draw a trend line. ALTARIS tests whether the line deserves belief, and argues against its own results before showing them. Each cell is checked with Mann–Kendall and Theil–Sen tests, adjusted for testing thousands of places at once (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR), stress-tested across many year windows, re-tested after removing El Niño/La Niña effects, and flagged for a possible jump around 2014, when the satellites changed. We calibrated the method on 1,000 simulated series: in pure noise, "consistent" never appeared (0.0 %), while a real 20 % decline per decade was detected 54 % of the time. The tool is deliberately cautious. We also report the other side: “limited evidence” appears in about a third of pure-noise series (33.1 %), which is why it is shown as an unconfirmed signal and not as a finding.

Results and honesty

196 cells (rainy season) pass every test, mainly in Costa Rica, Guatemala, Panama and Nicaragua; none in Honduras or El Salvador. We do not present this as a climate finding. Of the three guided examples, two show why. In Guatemala's highlands the decline passes every test, yet it concentrates around 2009, rain gauges are sparse and NASA POWER does not show it in that cell, so it remains an open question; consistent cells in Costa Rica and Panama show similar step-like changes around 2010–2012, and we infer no cause. As an independent check, one case (Choluteca, Honduras) was reproduced with NASA Giovanni from the same IMERG product: the Sen slope (−48.1 mm per decade) and its 95 % interval (−257.4 to +170.9) match our pipeline to the first decimal. This verifies the implementation for that case only. Another example shows how the chosen years can reverse the apparent direction of a trend. ALTARIS describes the past; it makes no forecasts, risk indices or causal claims.

Data, tools and process

Data: NASA GPM IMERG Final Run V07 monthly rainfall (0.1°, 2001–2024, GES DISC); NASA POWER for comparison at the case sites; NOAA CPC ONI for El Niño/La Niña; NASA GIBS (VIIRS imagery) and NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble for the opening globe; Natural Earth borders; and the Hipparcos/Yale star catalogue for the sky. Analysis: Python, NumPy, SciPy and pymannkendall. Interface: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and Recharts, deployed on Cloudflare. The code is open and the results are reproducible: decision thresholds were frozen before the expansion to seven countries, and the exported data records the engine version and every change.

Factors we considered

Satellite cells cannot capture hillside microclimates; fixed seasonal windows may not match each local rainy season; a 24-year record cannot separate a trend from decadal variability; windows overlap and neighbouring cells are correlated. We list these limits in the tool itself.

Use of AI

Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with code, tests, documentation, translation and the scripts that rendered the demo video. Cell narratives are produced with deterministic templates: no generative model computes statistics or assigns verdicts. Every image in the demo video is a real screen capture of the app; no images or video were generated. The background music is an original score synthesised with code and composed with AI assistance (Claude); it is AI-generated audio.

Source code: https://github.com/Joshua203-byte/Hackathon-NASA
